The small mammal Pere David's vole, Eothenomys melanogaster, exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its adaptation to montane environments across eastern Asia. In captive colony studies conducted at a stable body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the basal metabolic rate of adults was measured at 62.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 62.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that falls within the expected range for a murid rodent of its body size. This metabolic measurement was obtained under standard thermoneutral conditions and provides a baseline for understanding the species' energetic demands, which are likely influenced by the cool, humid microclimates of its dense understory habitat. The combination of a low neonatal mass and a moderate resting metabolism suggests a reproductive strategy that prioritizes rapid early development within the constraints of a relatively frugal energy budget.

The trajectory from a 2-gram birth mass to an adult body form is thus compressed into roughly two months.

This relatively extended lifespan for a small-bodied rodent is noteworthy, as many similarly sized murids rarely exceed 2 to 3 years in captivity. Such life-history traits distinguish E. melanogaster from many of its lowland congeners.
